text: Build a k by k matrix. Place each number from one to k exactly once; the rest are zero. A row condition a, b means a's row is strictly above b's row. Column conditions are the same idea for columns. Return any valid matrix, or an empty one if none exists.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — each number gets one cell. Its row is controlled only by the row conditions, and its column only by the column conditions. So the row and the column are two separate questions. Right? Here's the thing I want to say early. A is above b is just an order. It says a comes before b when I stack rows top to bottom. That's a topological order. Same for columns, left to right. Are there any constraints on k and on how many conditions there are?
k is up to four hundred, and each condition list has up to ten to the fourth entries. Conditions can contradict each other.

Good — can contradict tells me I must detect a cycle and return empty. Let me run through the example. Take k equals three, with row conditions one above two, and three above two. A valid top-to-bottom order is one, three, two. That gives one the top row, then three, then two.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to try every possible ordering of rows and columns and check the conditions. But that's k factorial orderings. With k up to four hundred, that's hopeless. This problem reminds me of topological sort. Each above or left rule is a directed edge. A valid line-up is a topo order of that graph. If the graph has a cycle, no order exists. The key move is to keep rows and columns separate. Two independent graphs, two independent topo sorts. Mixing them would invent fake cycles across dimensions that don't really conflict.

Here's the plan. I'm using Kahn's algorithm — peel off in-degree-zero nodes — to get each order. One: topo-sort the row conditions; the i-th number in that order sits in row i. Two: do the same for the column conditions to get each column. Three: if either order is shorter than k, there's a cycle, so return empty; otherwise drop each value at its row and column crossing. One thing worth flagging about correctness. Both position maps are permutations of zero to k minus one, so the k values land in k different cells — like a permutation matrix. No collisions, and every other cell is naturally zero. There's a trade-off here. The matrix itself costs k squared space, which I can't avoid since I have to return it. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Go ahead and code it up.

Alright, let me code this up. The main function runs topo twice, returns empty if either order comes back empty, records each number's row and column index, and drops it at that crossing. Topo is plain Kahn: build the edges, push every in-degree-zero number, and when popping a node drops a neighbor to zero, that neighbor joins the queue. One thing worth flagging in topo. The cycle check is the return line: order size equals k. In a clean DAG every node enters and leaves the queue once, so the order has all k nodes. If a cycle exists, those nodes never reach in-degree zero, so the order comes up short. That one comparison is my whole no-answer test.

Let's dry-run the code. k equals three; rows: one above two, three above two; columns: two left of one, three left of two. The moment it clicks is in the row sort: popping three drops two's in-degree to zero, so two gets freed and takes the last row. That free-a-node-when-its-last-prerequisite-leaves step is the heart of Kahn's. The row order is one, three, two; the column order is three, two, one. Dropping each value at its crossing gives a matrix where all four conditions check out. Let's also test with corner cases. One, two, three in a cycle — no node hits in-degree zero, topo comes back short, so I return empty. A repeated condition just bumps the in-degree twice and gets undone twice. A number in no condition starts at in-degree zero and can go anywhere.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is big O of k squared plus E, where E is the total number of conditions. Each topo sort is big O of k plus E; the k squared comes from building the k by k matrix, which I have to do anyway. Space is also big O of k squared plus E — the matrix is k squared, and the two graphs are k plus E. In the worst-case scenario, one dimension has all the edges, but Kahn still touches each node and edge once, so it stays linear in the graph. Oh, one more thing — if the caller only needs a yes or no answer, I can skip building the matrix entirely. Just run both topo sorts and return whether both succeeded. That drops it to big O of k plus E time and space.

Nice. Three things stood out. You saw early that rows and columns are independent, so two separate topo sorts, not one mixed graph. You reduced the cycle test to one clean line — order size equals k. And you argued no collisions from the permutation structure, instead of hand-waving it. Strong hire.
